newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan investors cautiously push up stock weighting.
newsitem.headline: Japan investors cautiously push up stock weighting.

text.p: Japanese institutional investors plan a cautious lifting of their weighting in stocks next month, wary of a Dow bubble but also afraid of missing out on the bull run, a Reuters investment survey showed on Thursday.
The survey asked 16 Japan-based institutions in late July about their investment strategy for August.
The average stock weighting rose 1.68 points to 48.50 percent, its second-highest level since Reuters began its monthly Global Asset Allocations surveys in March 1995.
Bond and cash average weightings were lowered, with bonds falling 0.34 of a point to 38.75 percent and cash down 1.34 points to 12.75 percent.

Within the stocks portfolio, the weighting for the United States rose 1.29 points to 40.70, although much of this was due to the addition to the survey of a new respondent with a high equities weighting.
Most investors were concerned that the Dow was somewhat overheated and said that in the medium to long term they were shifting to a more neutral stance.
"There's media reports worrying about company profits but the market's not reacting. Stocks seem to be a tad overheated," said a fund manager at Dowa Kasai.
Others said they could not help but be bullish in the short term.

"In the United States, low interest rates, good corporate results and strong demand for stocks continues," said an analyst at Daiwa Research Institute, who with many others forecast the Dow would rise to around 8,400 to 8,500 in August.
In contrast, investors saw little risk of a fall in the Nikkei average but they said there was strong resistance, especially around the 21,000 mark, to large upward pressure.

They said with Tokyo stocks apparently lagging behind other world stocks, money from overseas investors was expected to flow in to some extent but added that there was still uncertainty over the recovery and few obvious factors to push stocks higher.

Asian currency turmoil meant, however, that with the exception of Hong Kong, investors were less than enchanted with share prospects in the region. The average Asian stock weighting fell for the fifth month in a row by 1.12 points to 5.31 percent -- its lowest level since the survey began.
In Europe, German stocks continue to hug the spotlight, rising for the seventh consecutive month to 7.53 percent as investors cited low interest rates, corporate restructuring and a weak mark.

Within the bond portfolio, the weighting for Japan fell for the first time in two months, down 1.22 points to 15.22 percent. Investors said rates would rise, although there was firm support for the weighting on the belief that a rate increase will take place later rather than sooner.

"Even in the economy's best case scenario, the Bank of Japan is not going to raise rates before the end of the year. It's more likely to be the beginning of next year," said an analyst at Okasan Research.
U.S. Treasuries were seen as a stable market and possibly benefiting from European economic and monetary union worries, the average weighting rose 1.39 points to 39.34 percent.

"It looks like interest rates are not going to rise and there'll be some correction coming from that. In addition, exchange rates are stable and there's likely to be some funds flowing in on EMU worries," said Okasan's analyst.
